intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 8 units · tectonics to contours

Grade 12 is “geography of Eritrea in depth”. Grade 11 is the toolkit: how the crust moves, how water and wind carve, how people settle, then a first look at Eritrea’s place, relief and contour maps. Read each unit as a *story with a cause* — examiners mark the cause, not only the landform name.

intro_cards.title: Worked contour gradient
body: Two points: 1 200 m and 1 000 m. Map distance between them is 4 cm. Scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m).
Rise = 200 m. Run = 4 × 500 = 2 000 m. Gradient = 200/2000 = 1 in 10 (or 10%). Write both the fraction and a sentence: “For every 10 m walked horizontally you climb 1 m.”

units.title: Gradation by Rivers and Winds
units.intro: **Gradation** is the slow flattening of the land: high places are worn down (*degradation*) and low places are filled (*aggradation*). Agents: rivers, wind, waves (Unit 3), ice (less relevant here), and gravity (mass wasting). Tectonics builds; gradation sculpts.

cards.title: 2.1.1 Degradation force
body: Degradation (Denudation) is the lowering of land by weathering and erosion due to the action of sun, rain, wind, rivers, frost and ice.
The change that comes on the surface of the rock due to the change of weather is called **weathering**.
In other words, weathering is the breaking down of hard rocks due to change of weather.
Physical weathering (mechanical weathering) is the breaking down and disintegration of rocks by many factors such as temperature changes, physical action of water, animals and plants.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Aggradation
body: Aggradation (Deposition) is the raising of the height of land by the deposition of the weathered and eroded materials.
After a long period of consolidation, these sediments can form sedimentary rocks.

steps.text: Liquid water transitioning into crystalline solid ice undergoes volumetric expansion.

steps.text: The process involves rock sheets peeling off in concentric layers parallel to the surface.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is categorized as an external, gradational geomorphic force?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Distinguish geomorphic forces**
Internal (endogenous) forces build up topography from inside. External (exogenous) forces wear down topography from outside.

**Step 2: Categorize options**
Volcanism, faulting, and folding are internal tectonic forces. Running water is an external gradational force.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct exogenous agent is **Running water**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: By what percentage does water volume expand when it undergoes freezing inside rock crevices?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall frost action parameters**
Liquid water transitioning into crystalline solid ice undergoes volumetric expansion.

**Step 2: Identify expansion percentage**
Water volume expands by exactly $$10\%$$ upon freezing, producing the destructive pressure responsible for frost wedging.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The expansion is **$$10\%$$**.

cards.title: Quick check

options.B: wear down and level the Earth's surface, e.g. weathering, erosion and deposition
options.C: build up the land, e.g. folding and faulting
options.D: come only from inside the Earth

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Internal (endogenic) forces such as folding, faulting and volcanism build up relief.

**Step 2:** External (exogenic) gradational forces – weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition by water, wind, ice and waves – wear it down and fill low places.

**Step 3:** Answer: wearing down and levelling.

**Tip:** "Degradation" lowers land (erosion); "aggradation" builds it up by deposition – both are gradation.

cards.title: Gradation
body: **Gradation** is the levelling of the land surface by **degradation** (wearing down: weathering and erosion) and **aggradation** (building up by deposition). Agents: running water, wind, moving ice (glaciers), waves and groundwater; gravity also moves material downslope (mass wasting).

cards.title: 2.2.1 What is a rRiver?
body: **A river** is a flow of water in a natural channel.
Most rivers begin flowing from wet mountains, springs, lakes or melting snow.
The point where a river begins is called a **river source**.
At the river source, the river water flows in a tiny and narrow channel called a rill.

cards.title: 2.2.2 The work of a river
body: First, it erodes the land in a particular place.
Second, it deposits the eroded materials in other places.
Weathered materials due to physical weathering chemical weathering are is accumulated at the base of the parent rocks or hills.
The process of the washing away of the weathered material is called **sheet erosion**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the geomorphic term for the physical weathering process in which concentric rock shells peel off due to diurnal thermal expansion and contraction?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze process mechanics**
The process involves rock sheets peeling off in concentric layers parallel to the surface.

**Step 2: Link to thermal stress**
This is caused by daily solar heating (expansion) and nightly cooling (contraction) in arid environments, structurally defined as exfoliation.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct term is **Exfoliation**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which type of river load consists of soluble minerals traveling invisibly in solution?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Classify river load types**
River loads are divided into bed load, suspended load, and dissolved load.

**Step 2: Identify transport states**
Soluble minerals like calcium carbonate dissolve completely and travel invisibly. This is defined as the dissolved load.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct classification is **Dissolved load**.

cards.problem: Which type of river load consists of soluble minerals traveling invisibly in solution?

steps.text: River loads are divided into bed load, suspended load, and dissolved load.
Soluble minerals like calcium carbonate dissolve completely and travel invisibly. This is defined as the dissolved load.

cards.title: How rivers erode, transport and deposit
body: **Erosion:** hydraulic action (force of water), abrasion/corrasion (load scraping the bed), attrition (stones knocking together and becoming smaller and rounder), solution (dissolving soluble rocks such as limestone). **Transport:** traction (rolling big boulders), saltation (bouncing pebbles), suspension (fine particles carried in the water) and solution (dissolved minerals). **Deposition** happens when the river slows down and drops its load, for example on flood plains and in deltas.

steps.text: Soft rock undercuts; cap rock collapses.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The transportation of eroded materials **floats** in the river water like mud, silt and sand:
cards.why: **Suspended load** consists of very fine particles (clay, silt, and fine sand) that are held up by the turbulence of the water and 'float' within the stream as it flows.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The narrow, shallow channel cut in soil at a river's source is called a/an:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Trace river source structures**
At a river's headwaters, rainwater initially accumulates in tiny channels.

**Step 2: Identify channel dimensions**
These tiny channels, about $$5\text{ to } 8\text{ cm}$$ deep, are defined as rills.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct term is **Rill**.

cards.title: How a river works
body: A river has three jobs that happen together but dominate in different stretches.

1. **Erosion** — hydraulic action (the force of the water), abrasion (load scrapes the bed), attrition (stones smash each other smaller), solution (soluble rock dissolves).
2. **Transport** — dissolved load, suspended mud, saltation of sand, traction of cobbles along the bed. Faster, fuller rivers carry more and coarser load.
3. **Deposition** — when speed falls (inside of a bend, mouth, flood plain) the heaviest pieces drop first.

cards.title: A river grows old as the slope dies. Wadis in Eritrea often only run after rain — same three jobs, less water.
How a river works
body: **Upper course** (steep highland): vertical erosion, V-shaped valleys, interlocking spurs, potholes, waterfalls where hard rock sits over soft.

**Middle course:** lateral erosion starts to win. The channel swings into **meanders**. The outer bank is undercut (river cliff); the inner bank grows a point bar. A big flood may cut the neck and leave an ox-bow.

**Lower course:** gradient tiny, huge load of silt. Flood plain, levées, braided reaches, delta or estuary at the sea. Many Eritrean streams never reach a quiet old age — they are seasonal **wadis**: violent after rain, dry beds the rest of the year. Same three processes, pulsed.

**Wind** needs dry, loose sediment and weak plant cover — so it dominates semi-desert and desert. *Deflation* lifts fines and leaves a stony pavement. *Abrasion* sands the rock into yardangs and polished faces. Deposition builds dunes (shape depends on wind direction and sand supply) and can dump fine dust as loess far downwind. After overgrazing, wind finds more to eat — link this to Unit 5.

cards.title: Factors that decide how hard a river works
body: Volume (more rain or a bigger catchment), gradient (steeper = more energy), rock hardness, load already being carried, and vegetation on the banks. After a rare cloudburst a small Eritrean wadi can shift more gravel in one night than in the following six dry months. That is why bridges get wrecked and why farmers farm the wet bed anyway — the silt is a gift and a risk.

cards.title: 2.3.1 Upper stage
body: The upper stage of a river is usually found on mountainous areas where the slopes are steep.
The river water has high speed and few tributaries.
The work of the river is mainly erosion and transportation of its load.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Middle stage
body: The rate of erosion decreases, becausethe river flows slowly along a gentle slope.
In the middle part of middle course, the valley becomes wider by lateralerosion.
Open-V-shaped Valley: An open-V-shaped valley is formed due to vertical and lateral erosion.

cards.title: 2.3.3 Lower stage
body: In the lower Stage the river flows across a gentler slope or flat lands.
The river flows very slowly because the gradient is now very gentle or flat.
Due to the low velocity of the river, the river cannot transport the load further.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The geomorphic process where particles in a river's load collide with each other and break down into smaller, rounded shapes is called:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define channel erosion actions**
Fluvial erosion processes act on both the channel and the load itself.

**Step 2: Focus on sediment-sediment collision**
When rock fragments in the water collide with each other, wearing away their sharp edges, the process is defined as attrition.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The process is **Attrition**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In which stage of a river's course are V-shaped valleys and deep gorges primarily carved?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Match geomorphic zones to processes**
Deep down-cutting occurs where vertical erosion dominates.

**Step 2: Identify stage characteristics**
The Upper Stage has the steepest gradient and highest kinetic energy, driving intense vertical erosion that carves gorges and V-shaped valleys.

**Step 3: Final Result**
These features belong to the **Upper stage**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which statement is **incorrect** about the stages of a river?

options.A: Vertical erosion is dominant in upper stage.
options.B: Lateral erosion is dominant in the middle stage.
options.C: There are heavy erosion and little deposition in the lower stage.
options.D: Middle stage has many tributaries compared to upper stage.
options.E: The velocity of a river is very active at upper course.

cards.why: Statement C is incorrect because the **lower stage** of a river is characterized by **heavy deposition** and very little erosion. The river loses energy as it reaches flat land near the sea, causing it to drop its load.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A crescent-shaped lake formed when a river cuts straight through a narrow meander neck is called a/an:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Trace meander evolution**
During floods, highly curved meanders are bypassed at their narrow necks.

**Step 2: Identify the resulting feature**
When silt deposits seal off the old loop, it remains as an isolated crescent-shaped body of water called an ox-bow lake.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The lake is an **Ox-bow lake**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The natural raised embankments built along the banks of a lower-course river by flood deposits are known as:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze flooding processes**
During floods, sediment-laden water overflows the banks of a river.

**Step 2: Identify deposition zones**
Velocity drops immediately at the edges, depositing coarse sands first, which builds up raised ridges parallel to the channel called levees.

**Step 3: Final Result**
These raised banks are **Levees**.

cards.title: 2.4.1 What is the work of wind
body: Winds have tremendous force to cut off branches of trees and remove weathered materials from the surface of the earth.
The role of wind in changing the earth’s surface is more dominant in dry areas such as hot deserts and semi-deserts.
Deserts are also covered with rock waste that is produced by weathering of solid rocks.
Eventually, a surface layer of closely packed stone called a desert pavement is formed as the sand and silt are removed.

cards.title: 2.4.2 Features produced by wind erosion
body: The erosive work of winds depends on the quantity of sand particles the wind carries and the speed of the wind.
For example, strong winds can drive sand particles with a tremendous force against standing rocks for several kilometres.
The major noticeable features produced by wind action are as follows.
The top of the upstanding rock remains undisturbed and the lower portion is changed into a thin pillar.

cards.title: 2.4.3 Features produced by wind deposition
body: Winds also bounce grains of sand forward, which are deposited on the way.
The finest particles are deposited outside the desert region.
The largest particles are deposited within the desert regions.
The load is accumulated around the obstacle and forms a heap.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A series of waterfalls dropping along a single, continuous slope is geomorphically termed a/an:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze waterfall geomorphology**
Waterfalls are vertical drops. A single drop is a waterfall.

**Step 2: Define multiple sequential drops**
When multiple waterfalls occur in sequence along a single slope, they are classified as cataracts.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct term is **Cataract**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: A series of waterfalls dropping along a single, continuous slope is geomorphically termed a/an:

steps.text: Waterfalls are vertical drops. A single drop is a waterfall.
When multiple waterfalls occur in sequence along a single slope, they are classified as cataracts.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the geomorphic name for the twisting, winding curves formed by a river in its middle stage?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify middle stage landforms**
In the middle stage, lateral erosion widens the valley, and the river flows in winding curves.

**Step 2: Recall terminology**
These wide, twisting loops and bends are called meanders.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The loops are called **Meanders**.

steps.text: In the middle stage, lateral erosion widens the valley, and the river flows in winding curves.

cards.q: The type of erosion in a desert area where sand and dust particles are removed by wind is
cards.why: Deflation is the process by which wind blows across a loose surface, lifting and removing small, dry particles like silt and sand, often leaving behind a 'desert pavement' of larger stones.

cards.title: 2.5 Types of Desert Landscapes
body: Stony Desert: This is part of desert that is covered by sheets of angular gravel and pebbles.
Rocky Desert (Hamada): This is made of a bare rock pavement or zeugen.

cards.title: The three desert surfaces
body: Wind erosion, transport and deposition give hot deserts three main kinds of surface. Only about a fifth of the world's deserts is sand; most is stone or bare rock.
**Sand desert (erg):** a wide, undulating sea of sand sheets and dunes built by wind deposition, such as the great ergs of the Sahara. Dunes move slowly downwind and can bury roads and farms.

**Stony desert (reg in Algeria, serir in Libya):** a plain covered with angular gravel and pebbles. Deflation has blown the fine sand and dust away, leaving stones too heavy for the wind to lift – a "desert pavement".
**Rocky desert (hamada):** bare rock surfaces swept clean by the wind, often with rock pedestals, zeugen and yardangs carved by abrasion.
In Eritrea, sand and gravel surfaces occur in the hot, dry coastal plains and the Danakil, where wind and occasional flash floods shape the land.

cards.title: Identify a desert surface from a description
cards.problem: A traveller crosses a flat plain covered with angular pebbles. There is almost no loose sand, and the stones fit closely together. Which desert landscape is this, and how was it formed?

steps.text: **Step 1: Note the clues.** Flat plain, angular pebbles, almost no sand.
**Step 2: Match the surface.** Sand sheets and dunes = erg; bare rock = hamada; gravel and pebbles = reg (stony desert).
**Step 3: Explain the process.** Deflation removed the fine sand and dust, leaving stones too heavy for the wind: a desert pavement.

cards.answer: A stony desert (reg or serir), formed when deflation blew away the fine material and left the heavy pebbles behind.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which one of the following is **not** true about the desert landscape?
cards.why: All the pairs listed are correct terminology for desert types. **Erg** is a sand desert, **Hamada** is a rocky plateau, and both **Serir** and **Reg** refer to stony or gravel deserts. Therefore, none of the statements are 'not true'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A desert surface covered with angular gravel and pebbles, from which the wind has removed the fine sand, is called ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Deflation blows away sand and dust but cannot lift heavy stones.

**Step 2:** The remaining gravel surface is a stony desert, called reg in Algeria and serir in Libya.

**Step 3:** An erg is a sand sea; a hamada is bare rock.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which desert landscape is a wide sea of sand sheets and dunes?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Wind deposition builds sand sheets and dunes.

**Step 2:** A large area of them is called an erg (sand desert).

**Step 3:** Reg is stony, hamada is rocky, and a wadi is a dry valley.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

tips.text: Nothing that we see is permanent Tectonic forces increase the height of the surface of the earth. These are internal forces that originate from the interior of the earth. There are also external forces that reduce the heights of mountains, plateaus and hills.
These are accomplished by rivers, winds, wave actions, and glacial actions. These elements of external forces reduce the surface of the earth by wearing and erosion.
The external forces that change the surface of the earth is associated with erosion. These external forces that raise or lower the level lands are collectively called gradational forces.
Gradational force has two parts, namely, degradation and aggradation.
Degradation is the lowering away of land by weathering and erosion.
Aggradation is the increase of the height of land by deposition.
Rivers and winds modify the earth’s surface by eroding, transporting, and depositing the eroded materials. Both rivers and winds have features produced by their erosive action and deposition action.
The course of a river is divided into three stages. These are the upper course (steep-sided course), middle course (gentle slope), and lower course (flat land).
The action of the river in the three stages varies.
In the upper course, the action is erosion and transporting the eroded materials.

questions.q: Physical weathering is the breaking down and disintegration of rocks by?
why: Physical (mechanical) weathering involves the physical breaking of rocks without changing their chemical composition. This can be caused by **temperature changes** (expansion/contraction), **water action** (freeze-thaw), **plant roots** growing in cracks, and **animal activities** (burrowing).

questions.q: Which one of the following statements is **wrong**?

options.A: deposition is the main work of a river at lower course.
options.B: at the middle course the speed of the river is slower than the upper course.
options.C: load is the eroded materials carried out by a river.
options.D: the upper course of a river is the steepest of all courses.
options.E: erosion and transportation are the main work of a river at the lower course.

why: Statement E is wrong because at the **lower course**, the river's energy is low, and its primary work is **deposition**, not erosion and transportation. Erosion and transportation are the dominant processes in the upper and middle courses.

questions.q: Which of the following is **not** an external force?
why:
**Step 1: Define Geomorphic Processes.** Processes that shape the Earth's surface are divided into Endogenic (Internal) and Exogenic (External).
**Step 2: Identify External Forces.** External forces originate above the Earth's crust, such as weathering, erosion, and deposition by agents like water, wind, and ice.
**Step 3: Identify Internal Forces.** Internal forces originate within the Earth, such as volcanism and tectonism (folding/faulting). Therefore, Volcanism is not an external force.
